newsitem.title: ROMANIA: ROMANIA'S KING RETURNS HOME FROM EXILE.
newsitem.headline: ROMANIA'S KING RETURNS HOME FROM EXILE.

text.p: Romania's exiled King Michael returns to his homeland on Friday, with his citizenship restored by a government keen to use his prestige to enhance its longshot bid for quick NATO membership.
Michael's visit, his second home since being forced to abdicate by Soviet-backed communists nearly 50 years ago, is described officially as private.

But it includes dinner at what was once a royal palace with President Emil Constantinescu, whose election victory last November ended seven years of rule by ex-communists opposed to and fearful of Michael's return.

"I invited him (Michael) to Cotroceni next Tuesday. I'm looking forward to talking to a man who played a prominent role in Romanian and Europe's history," Constantinescu told state television ahead of the visit.
Prime Minister Victor Ciorbea and cabinet members are also expected to invite Michael to lunch on Saturday.
Michael, 75, will be handed a new Romanian passport on his arrival at Bucharest's Otopeni airport. Greeting him alongside cabinet members will be his former chauffeur and a schoolmate.

He then proceeds to his hotel, a lakeside villa where he signed his abdication at gunpoint in 1947, and lays a wreath in University Square, where protesters were killed in the 1989 uprising that toppled communist dictator Nicolae Ceausescu.
In a message preceding his visit, a week after having his citizenship returned, Michael said his intention was to give Romanians whatever he could.
He promised to respect Romania's 1991 republican constitution, which makes no provision for the monarchy, and submit no claims to property nationalised under the communists.

"As a simple citizen and former king, with prestige and relatives in European monarchies, he could be an ambassador at large, raising money for instance," Neagu Djuvara, a historian and monarchist, who returned to Romania in 1990, told Reuters.

Constantinescu has suggested Michael could use that influence to win an early entry ticket to an enlarged NATO alongside favourites Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic. Six NATO members, he says, are constitutional monarchies.
Many Romanians revere Michael for his courage as a young monarch during World War Two, when he arrested fascist leader Marshal Ion Antonescu and switched Romania to the Allied side.
On his first return from Switzerland in 1992, Michael drew hundreds of thousands into the streets on Orthodox Easter.

His subsequent visits were blocked by ex-communist president Ion Iliescu, who treated him as a foreign commoner and made the granting of a visa contingent on his public acceptance of the constitution.
Romanian state television plans to broadcast most of the king's engagements live.

It is uncertain how enthusiastic his reception will be this time, with a government favourable to him in power and many Romanians preoccupied with plunges in living standards which have left them far behind other east European states.

Only a small fraction of Romanians favour restoration of the king, who will be accompanied by his wife, Ana of Bourbon Parma, and his eldest daughter, Princess Margareta, who married a Romanian actor last year.
But an exhibition of photographs taken by the king in exile attracted large crowds at its opening on Thursday.
The ex-communists, thrown into opposition last year, have denounced the visit as an atempt to distract Romanians from price rises for utilities and staples introduced this month.
And nationalist parties have also criticised it as leaving the door open for constitutional ambiguity. REUTER
